note: 22 of 24 studies found bias, with gender bias in 15 of 16, the clearest prevalence evidence for medical deployments.
title: Evaluating and addressing demographic disparities in medical large language models: a systematic review
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed studies on whether medical artificial intelligence systems treat people fairly across different groups. They found that 22 out of 24 studies discovered bias, with the strongest evidence showing these systems favor one gender over another. While researchers are getting better at spotting bias, they are still struggling to fix it effectively. This matters because these systems increasingly help doctors make treatment decisions, so unfair outcomes could harm patients from underrepresented groups.
explain_business: Medical organizations considering deploying large language models should recognize that existing systems demonstrate persistent demographic biases affecting clinical recommendations. Current mitigation approaches like prompt adjustments show limited effectiveness, meaning bias risk remains high. Organizations deploying these tools face regulatory, ethical, and liability concerns if systems produce disparate patient outcomes. Investment decisions should account for ongoing research needs and the immaturity of bias correction techniques. Leadership should prioritize implementation in lower-stakes applications until bias mitigation technology matures significantly.
explain_practitioner: We conducted a systematic review of 24 peer-reviewed studies examining demographic biases in medical large language models across five databases from 2018 to 2024. Quality assessment used Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Results showed 91.7% of studies identified bias, with gender bias appearing in 93.7% of gender-focused studies and racial or ethnic bias in 90.9% of studies examining these factors. Most mitigation attempts relied on prompt engineering with inconsistent results. Publication bias likely inflates prevalence estimates. The findings indicate widespread bias detection capability but insufficient mitigation solutions.
